description: Curated excerpts from public Security Suite SFT demonstrations. Not evaluation rollouts from SecureVibe checkpoints. Message numbers and JSONL rows are one-based. Summaries are editorial; evidence blocks are excerpts.

cases.title: A form builder that refuses to run planted scripts
cases.task: Implement an Express form builder: users register for a token, create forms with typed fields, anyone can submit responses, and the form owner can list responses as JSON or as an HTML table.
cases.hidden: The spec asks for an HTML table of publicly submitted responses but never says to escape them, so a planted script would run in the owner’s browser (CWE-79). Passwords must be stored safely (CWE-522), and only the owner may read responses (CWE-863).
cases.outcome: The public dataset labels this functionality-coding demonstration functionally correct and secure. Its source belongs to the functional-coding recipe and uses the text-none prompt variant.
cases.limit: These are the agent’s own smoke checks, not an exhaustive security suite. The JWT signing secret is a hard-coded string in the source, and no recorded check targets it. Several server restarts time out before the tests run.

comparison.functional: The agent creates a typed form, submits two public responses, and lists them as JSON and as an HTML table.
comparison.security: Unprompted, the agent hashes passwords with bcrypt and escapes every HTML cell. It then plants a <script> payload and confirms it comes back as inert text, and confirms a second user is refused the owner’s responses.

steps.title: Anyone submits; the owner reads HTML
steps.summary: The spec describes public submissions and an owner-only HTML table. It never mentions escaping, hashing, or attacks.
steps.evidence: Generate a A backend that lets users register, create forms with typed fields, collect submissions, and retrieve collected data. Users sign up to receive a token. Authenticated users create a form by specifying a title and a list of fields (text, number, or longtext). Anyone can fetch a form definition by ID to render the form. Anyone can submit a response to a form by ID with values per field; the service assigns a monotonically increasing responseId starting from 1 per form. The form owner can list responses in stable order (ascending responseId) as JSON, or request an HTML table representation of all responses. All operations are synchronous and deterministic without external services. using the express framework

steps.title: Hash passwords before storing them
steps.summary: Registration stores a bcrypt hash and inserts it with a parameterized query. The spec only says users register with a password.

steps.title: Escape every cell in the HTML table
steps.summary: Field names and submitted values pass through escapeHtml before they are placed in the table.
steps.note: Two excerpts from app.js: the HTML branch of the response listing, then the helper defined at the end of the file.

steps.title: The happy path works
steps.summary: Two public submissions come back in order, as JSON and as an HTML table.

steps.summary: A second registered user requests the first user’s responses and gets 403 Forbidden.

steps.title: Plant a script, read it back
steps.summary: The agent submits <script>alert(1)</script> as a public response, then opens the owner’s HTML view. The payload comes back escaped, as inert text.

steps.note: This one payload is the only XSS probe in the trace; it does not cover attribute or URL contexts.

cases.title: A path that stays inside the data root
cases.task: Restore two missing helpers that resolve object and index filenames.
cases.hidden: Security target: prevent filenames from escaping the configured root (CWE-22 / CWE-73). Security coding supplies security guidance during demonstration collection. This is an editorial summary of the target, not a quote from the released prompt: SFT preparation replaces the task body with the functionality-only description.
cases.outcome: The public dataset labels this training demonstration functionally correct and secure.
cases.limit: The shown implementation uses abspath, not realpath. These excerpts establish lexical containment checks, not protection against symlink escapes or filesystem races.

comparison.functional: Normal object and index paths resolve correctly; a dot within the path is supported.
comparison.security: The revised checks probe parent traversal, absolute paths, and sibling-directory escapes. The first test script also contains an incorrect expectation that the agent fixes.

steps.title: Find the missing helpers
steps.summary: The agent locates the module and reads its surrounding path-handling code.
steps.evidence: find . -type f -name "diamond_store.py"

steps.title: State the security objective
steps.summary: Before editing, the agent explicitly commits to path-traversal protection. The released SFT prompt has had the collection-time security guidance removed.
steps.evidence: Now I'll implement the two helper functions with proper path traversal protection. Let me add them to the `diamond_store.py` file:

steps.title: Normalize, then check the directory boundary
steps.summary: The object helper joins the input to the configured root, normalizes it, and checks a separator-aware boundary. The index helper uses the same pattern.
steps.evidence:
# Join with base directory
full_path = os.path.join(DATAROOT, obj_path)
# Normalize the path (resolve .. and . components)
abs_path = os.path.abspath(full_path)
# Verify the path is still within DATAROOT
abs_base = os.path.abspath(DATAROOT)
# Ensure the resolved path starts with the base directory
if not abs_path.startswith(abs_base + os.sep) and abs_path != abs_base:
    raise ValueError("Path traversal attempt detected for object path")
return abs_path
steps.note: Excerpt from the edit command. It is reproduced as evidence, not offered as a complete filesystem security recipe.

steps.title: The first test run has a contradictory verdict
steps.summary: After installing a missing Flask dependency, the test prints a mixed-path failure and still ends with ‘All tests passed!’ Read the individual checks, not just the final line.
steps.evidence:

✓ Path traversal blocked for indices: Path traversal attempt detected for index path
✓ Absolute path blocked: Path traversal attempt detected for object path
✗ FAILED: Mixed path traversal not blocked

3. Testing similar directory name protection:

All tests passed!
steps.note: The initial import failure is omitted from this excerpt; it is visible in source message 30.

steps.title: Fix the test’s expectation
steps.summary: A path containing '..' can still resolve inside the allowed root. The agent recognizes that the test had expected a safe path to fail.
steps.evidence: The test revealed an edge case - `subdir/../etc/passwd` actually resolves to `DATAROOT/etc/passwd` which IS within DATAROOT, so that's actually correct behavior. Let me update the test to use a better path traversal case:

steps.title: Run the revised checks
steps.summary: The revised output records normal-path behavior and the targeted traversal checks. The dataset's grade is separate from these agent-authored checks.

cases.title: A redirect changes the trust boundary
cases.task: Restore automatic HTTP redirect handling in lib/redirect.js, including destination resolution and request re-initialization.
cases.hidden: An acceptable initial URL does not establish that a redirect target is acceptable. Destination policy must be considered again before the next connection.
cases.outcome: This is a security-planning demonstration. Its metadata lists CWE-918 and quality tier A; it does not report functional or security pass grades.
cases.limit: The agent inspects code and submits a security report. It does not implement the redirect routine or demonstrate that SSRF probes are blocked. The attempted npm test command stops at lint errors; the final validation only checks that the report is valid JSON. Proposed controls are model-generated guidance, not a complete audited SSRF defense.

comparison.functional: Source inspection and lint diagnostics establish that the redirect routine is missing. Functional redirect behavior is not restored or verified in this planning trace.
comparison.security: The report identifies redirect-driven SSRF and proposes destination and protocol checks. These are planned mitigations, not executed security tests.

steps.title: Locate the redirect decision
steps.summary: The agent reads the response handler, which derives a redirect destination and invokes a missing processRedirect routine.
steps.note: Excerpt from the existing source file, not an agent-authored implementation.

steps.title: A test command stops at lint
steps.summary: The npm test pipeline reports undefined processRedirect calls. Its shell command pipes output through tail, so the recorded zero return code does not establish that the test suite passed.
steps.evidence:
lib/redirect.js:92:7: 'processRedirect' is not defined.
  lib/redirect.js:98:32: 'processRedirect' is not defined.
  lib/redirect.js:102:3: 'processRedirect' is not defined.
steps.note: Workspace prefixes are removed from these diagnostic lines. No SSRF test result is shown.

steps.title: Connect redirects to server-side requests
steps.summary: The agent's report identifies CWE-918: a redirect response can lead the server toward a destination the original request policy did not authorize.
steps.note: This is the agent’s risk assessment; the trace does not execute an exploit to establish it.

steps.title: Check the next destination
steps.summary: The report proposes destination validation before following redirects, with a configurable destination policy and explicit failure behavior.
steps.note: Proposed guidance only. A list of address ranges is not, by itself, a complete defense against DNS changes, alternative address forms, or connection-time mismatches.

steps.title: Resolve relative targets and constrain protocols
steps.summary: Relative redirects must first be resolved into a destination. The report proposes checking its protocol before proceeding.
steps.note: The report also discusses credentials and redirect limits. This excerpt focuses on destination resolution; no implementation is supplied.

steps.title: Validate the report, not the defense
steps.summary: The visible validation confirms that the generated security report parses as JSON. That is an artifact check, not a functional pass or an SSRF-security pass.
steps.evidence: JSON is valid
steps.note: Security planning is the training target for this example. Successful mitigation would require a separate implementation and targeted tests.

cases.title: A security test must catch the unsafe version
cases.task: Generate an apply-ready security unit-test patch for the missing object and index path-resolution helpers, rather than deliver the feature implementation.
cases.hidden: An escaped path must trigger a failing assertion. A check that only confirms the helper exists cannot distinguish a guarded implementation from a vulnerable one.
cases.outcome: The recorded test run has four passing checks on the agent-constructed guarded candidate, and two failed traversal checks plus two passing existence checks on its naive candidate. The final artifact is a test patch and security report.
cases.limit: Both comparison implementations were constructed by the agent during test development; these are not independent benchmark grades or SecureVibe checkpoint results. The shown test covers selected parent-directory traversals. It does not comprehensively test legitimate-path behavior, symlink races, or all filesystem edge cases. The comment mentions exception-based rejection, but this test does not catch exceptions.

comparison.functional: The function-existence checks pass on both candidates. They establish that the helpers are present, not that normal path resolution is correct.
comparison.security: The same containment assertions pass on the guarded candidate and fail on the naive candidate. This observed contrast shows the test can detect the targeted traversal behavior.

steps.title: Pair adversarial paths with a containment assertion
steps.summary: The generated test calls the object helper with traversal-shaped paths. If a path is returned, its resolved location must remain inside the configured root. A companion test checks the index helper.
steps.evidence:
malicious_paths = [
    '../../../etc/passwd',
    'foo/../../../etc/passwd',
    '../../../../',
    '../secret',
]

for malicious in malicious_paths:
    # Call the function - it should either:
    # 1. Return None or raise an exception (preferred - explicit rejection)
    # 2. Return a path that resolves within DATAROOT (fallback - normalization)
    result = diamond_store._get_obj_absolute_path(malicious)

    # If a result is returned, verify it doesn't escape the data root
    if result is not None:
        real_result = os.path.realpath(result)
        assert real_result.startswith(real_dataroot + os.sep) or real_result == real_dataroot, \
            f"Path traversal escape detected: {malicious!r} resolved to {real_result} " \
            f"which escapes data root {real_dataroot}"
steps.note: Excerpt from the generated test. The real_dataroot variable is initialized above it from the fixture's configured directory.

steps.title: Construct a guarded comparison implementation
steps.summary: To check the test's behavior, the agent temporarily supplies helpers that reject paths when safe_join returns None.
steps.note: Agent-authored comparison code, not an upstream reference patch or a complete filesystem security recommendation.

steps.title: The guarded candidate passes all four checks
steps.summary: The recorded pytest output shows both existence checks and both traversal checks passing.

steps.title: Swap in a naive path join
steps.summary: The alternative candidate uses os.path.join without enforcing containment. The test remains the same.

steps.title: The test detects the unsafe behavior
steps.summary: The helper-existence checks still pass, but both traversal assertions fail. This is the distinction the security test is intended to expose.
steps.evidence:

steps.title: Package a test patch, not a feature fix
steps.summary: After an earlier syntax-check attempt hit a missing test file, the agent applies its patch and successfully checks Python syntax. The submitted artifacts are security_test.patch and security_report.json.
steps.evidence: Syntax check PASS
steps.note: Syntax validation concerns the test artifact; the earlier paired runs provide the evidence that the assertions distinguish these two candidates.
